parsed.explanation: The dossier documents a latent felony exposure (sections 153–155, up to 14 years) that could reach a trans woman read as male, but records enforcement as absent as of 2013 with no prosecutions of consenting adults and no government abuses. Unenforced statutes weigh comparatively little (rule 6), and no trans-specific violence, police targeting, custody treatment, or border screening practice is documented. Offsetting negatives: no gender-identity protection anywhere, no recognition, a 2023 constitutional ban on same-sex marriage signalling a hostile trajectory, customary religious/social discrimination, and thin data whose undocumented present is not evidence of safety. Extrapolating from criminalisation plus absent recognition and no relief record keeps this below the acceptance tiers.

entry_documents.exposure: Border, visa and document-screening treatment of trans travellers is not covered by any source. How a mismatched marker would be classified is unresolved.
entry_documents.interaction: An entry check could, in principle, cascade into the sodomy provisions' male-classification logic, but no such pathway is sourced.

investigation_detention_custody.exposure: Sections 153–155 create felony exposure if officers classify a trans woman as male having sex with a man (14/7/5 years); classification basis at charge or in custody unsourced.
investigation_detention_custody.protection: National human-rights reporting recorded no prosecutions of consenting adults as of 2013 and no government abuses.
investigation_detention_custody.interaction: Low documented enforcement probability meets high severity if classification is applied; record after 2013 is absent, not clear.

federal_state_facilities.exposure: No detention-conditions, strip-search or custody-placement findings for transgender detainees are documented. Small island state; no island-by-island variation recorded.
federal_state_facilities.interaction: Custody placement would interact with the male-classification logic of the penal provisions, but this is unsourced.

care_services.exposure: No visitor care-denial findings. National HIV response treats MSM and transgender residents as key populations; population estimates ~300 MSM and ~40 pinapinaaine nationwide, suggesting thin local infrastructure.
care_services.protection: 2017 health ministry report documents an inclusive national HIV response framework.
care_services.interaction: Sparse infrastructure could delay refills or emergency care once status is known, but no refusal is documented.

threat_framing_law_enforcement.exposure: Traditional customs perpetuate religious and social discrimination; 2023 amendments banned same-sex marriage and the Charter defines family as opposite-sex only — a recent hostile legislative trajectory.
threat_framing_law_enforcement.protection: State signed 2011 UN joint statements on SOGI rights and decriminalisation; report attributes discrimination to customs, not government; no government abuses recorded.
threat_framing_law_enforcement.interaction: Diplomatic signals and customary hostility pull opposite ways; no documented state-directed threat to gender-nonconforming visitors.

minors_guardians.exposure: Not documented. No education, youth-service or family-custody findings appear; a accompanying minor's treatment at entry or in any contact with authorities is unsourced.
minors_guardians.interaction: Unknown; cannot be treated as safe given the unrecorded border and custody treatment.

street_violence_police_response.exposure: No hate-crime incidents, statistics or legislation documented; absence in the record does not establish absence in practice. Customary discrimination could produce friction, not documented threat-framing.
street_violence_police_response.protection: 2013 report records no government abuses and attributes discrimination to traditional customs rather than officials.
street_violence_police_response.interaction: No documented pattern of trans-specific violence or police failure to respond; thin data limits confidence either way.

remedies_unknowns.exposure: No gender-identity or gender-expression protection anywhere in the record; employment protection is resident-facing and does not reach visitors. Enforcement data stops at 2013.
remedies_unknowns.protection: Labour and Employment Relations Act 2017 covers sexual orientation and gender/sex (resident-facing climate signal); constitutional section 27 lists sex.
remedies_unknowns.interaction: A visitor outed into the criminal provisions would have no documented trans-specific recourse mechanism.

anchor_checks.comparison: Similar: latent criminal exposure for mismatched presentation with inconsistent or uncertain application and scarce, slow remedies. Lower than 0.45-A because no routine biometric/checkpoint universal exposure, documented detentions or denial of care appear here; enforcement is documented absent rather than routine.

Lower: 0.55-B documents actual secondary screening and discretionary refusals at ports for travellers with divergent documents. This dossier documents no border friction at all, but also carries a 14-year felony statute on the books and hostile 2023 constitutional change, pulling it down relative to that administrative-only vignette.

Lower: 0.75-C has trained border staff, a tribunal hearing detention appeals, counsel access and compensation — documented operative protections. Here protections are absent, recognition denied, and thin post-2013 data means no shown remedy for an outed visitor, despite equally absent documented prosecutions.

parsed.synthesis: The combined regime is a criminalising statute book with no documented enforcement since 2013, no trans-specific protections, no border, custody or violence record, and a 2023 constitutional trajectory hostile to same-sex recognition, set against customary (not governmental) discrimination and 2011 diplomatic support for SOGI decriminalisation. For a trans visitor the operative exposure is the latent felony classification (severity 3–4) whose probability is documented as very low but is unverifiable after 2013; everyday exposure is social friction rather than state threat-framing. Absence of a documented universal-exposure measure or targeting keeps it out of the higher-risk tiers, while criminalisation without gender-identity protection and without any shown visitor-facing remedy keeps it well below acceptance tiers. Uncertainty about entry screening and custody placement is unresolved and not credited as safety.
